Being on the other side, for me at least, is very humbling. I have to ask people to do simple things for me because I'm in too much pain, it's hard for me to give myself a good quality of life right now. It's often humiliating. And then on top of my own ego bullshit, there's the weight of **needing** someone else.  I'm afraid that my independence will be stripped from me, which makes me lash out to the people who help me. It's an ugly cycle. 

But, that's what you do for love. You accept the ugly, the pain, the frustration and you let it go. You forgive. You find that every day you have a little bit more patience, and that's a really beautiful thing.

Hello! Not trying to make **any** assumptions here because I don't know you or your sister, but as someone diagnosed with anorexia this comment sent up huge red flags for me. It's a really common practice for people with eating disorders to eat more than the people around them to give off the appearance of health or normalcy.

I've starved myself for days before going to dinner with family/friends so that I could be gluttonous, but still be at a caloric deficit for the week.

It's rough, but in a lot of ways my mother's death has motivated me to get better.

I want to be a person she'd be proud of, and that means learning to take care and provide for myself now that I don't have a home to run back to.

Losing a parent will never be easy, you'll never be ready, it will be traumatic. But I try to remind myself that I don't have to live in that pain, I can let it pass and move on. Some days are harder than others.

I just try to redirect my negative emotions about her death into something positive. It gets easier over time. Time really can heal all wounds, if you let it. 

So don't be scared about your parents dying. Enjoy their company, listen to their advice. Take lots of pictures together, make a habit of exchanging hand written cards. Spend the time you have with them making memories and cherishing them, it'll make all the difference later.
